To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) Cu-thionein from yeast cells is a Cu(I)-S-rich protein; (ii) Cu-thioneins from yeast cells and in vitro are very similar in their chemical and physico-chemical properties; (iii) Cu-thioneinin yeast cells can be isolated in a Cu(I) form and (iv) Cu(I) thionein from yeast is an important Cu(I)-S rich protein for copper transport.
Cu(I)-thioneins are stable Cu(I)-S rich complexes that are able to bind and transport copper in a safe manner, and that they are released from cells when needed.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of copper metabolism in copper-resistant yeasts, with particular attention to the intracellular fate of copper.
the characterization of Cu-thionein, a copper storage protein, from the copper-resistant yeast strain X 218-1Aa.
copper(I)-thioneins, a new class of proteins which are found in the cells of copper-resistant yeast strains, and which have been isolated in the form of Cu(I)-thioneine.

the Cu-thionein from the copper-loaded yeast cells is identical with the Cu-thionei from copper-loaded cells of the wild-type strain X 21801Aa.
the Cu-thionein released from copper-loaded yeast is identical to the intracellular protein.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
copper-loaded cells of the copper-tolerant yeast strain X 218O-1Aa contain a protein which is identical to the Cu-thionein of copper-sensitive yeast strains.

The main takeaway from our work is that
Cu-thionein is a very effective carrier for copper transport in the cell.
